notes.canopy: Tree canopy is the one feature that rises with Black population share. The paper reads this as unmanaged vegetation on vacant lots rather than urban greening - compare against vacant housing units to see the confound.

evidence.quote: Sidewalks just end; the bike lane disappears after two blocks.
evidence.theme: 1.3 Spatial disparities in the built environment
evidence.pairs_with: The VLM classified cycling infrastructure as present on 87.8% of segments. Against human audits it agreed on 5.5% of panoramas (AC1 -0.88) and was excluded from all analyses.

evidence.quote: North City feels forgotten—bad housing, no grocery, heavy traffic.
evidence.pairs_with: Each 1-point rise in a tract's share of Black residents predicts 0.24 fewer percentage points of well-maintained buildings and 0.24 fewer of continuous pavement (both p < 0.001).

evidence.quote: Tower Grove has shade, cafés, safe crossings—everything works together.
evidence.pairs_with: Related features do cluster as the quotation describes: high tree canopy is more common on segments with a park nearby (57.8% vs 50.2%), and graffiti is rarer where facades are well maintained (2.4% vs 8.1%).

evidence.quote: The architecture is stunning, but the next street looks bombed-out.
evidence.pairs_with: Facade maintenance has the widest tract-level spread of any retained feature: tract values run from 26.5% to 100% well-maintained.

evidence.quote: There are 90 municipalities here. Nobody wants to work together—it's city versus city.
evidence.pairs_with: Fragmented governance is offered as the mechanism behind the spatial pattern; the audit measures the outcome, not the cause.

evidence.quote: We use tree canopy maps and overlay them with ER visits and asthma rates—it makes the inequities visible.
evidence.pairs_with: Tree canopy runs opposite to every other feature: +0.10 points per 1-point rise in Black population share (p < 0.01). Tract vacancy is the likely confound—switch the comparison to vacancy to see it.
